title: The Communist Manifesto
author: Karl Marx & Friedrich Engels
openingText: A spectre is haunting Europe—the spectre of Communism. All the Powers of old Europe have entered into a holy alliance to exorcise this spectre: Pope and Czar, Metternich and Guizot, French Radicals and German police-spies. Where is the party in opposition that has not been decried as Communistic by its opponents in power? Where is the Opposition that has not hurled back the branding reproach of Communism, against the more advanced opposition parties, as well as against its reactionary adversaries? Two things result from this fact. I. Communism is already acknowledged by all European Powers to be itself a Power.
about:
The Communist Manifesto is a 30-page political pamphlet published in February 1848 by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, on the eve of the European revolutions of that year. It argues that all history is the history of class struggle, that capitalism is a necessary but transient stage that creates the conditions for its own overthrow, and that the workers of the world must unite to abolish private ownership of the means of production.

The Manifesto was commissioned by the Communist League. It became the most widely read political text of the 19th and 20th centuries — translated into every major language, distributed by millions, and the founding document of communist movements that reshaped much of the world. Whether one agrees with it or not, it is impossible to understand modern political history without it.

angleCards.title: The bourgeois revolution is incomplete.
angleCards.text: Marx does not simply attack the bourgeoisie — he spends several pages admiring it. The bourgeoisie has been the most revolutionary class in history, dissolving feudalism, creating the world market, dragging every nation into modernity. Read Part I asking: what does Marx think the bourgeoisie actually achieved, and why does that achievement contain the seed of its own undoing?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Manifesto through Marx's ambivalent admiration for the bourgeoisie — understanding what it created, why that creation was historically necessary, and how the very forces it unleashed produce the conditions for its overthrow.

angleCards.title: Class struggle as the engine of history.
angleCards.text: The opening sentence is the thesis: the history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles. Every political conflict, every war, every cultural transformation is, for Marx, a surface expression of deeper antagonisms between economic classes. Read asking whether the historical examples he gives actually support the framework — and where the framework strains.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace Marx's historical-materialist argument through the Manifesto — testing the claim that class struggle is the primary driver of historical change against the specific examples he gives, and asking what the framework explains and what it misses.

angleCards.title: The 10-point program.
angleCards.text: Part II ends with a concrete list: ten demands the Communists would immediately enact upon seizing power. A graduated income tax. Free education. Abolition of child labour. Centralisation of credit in a national bank. Read the list and note how many of its demands are now enacted in liberal democracies — and ask what that means for the revolutionary argument.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Manifesto's practical program — the ten demands of Part II — and track which have been absorbed into ordinary liberal governance, which remain radical, and what that absorption says about the relationship between revolutionary politics and reform.

angleCards.title: The cash nexus.
angleCards.text: The most vivid passage in the Manifesto describes how the bourgeoisie has drowned every human bond — religious devotion, chivalry, family sentiment — in the icy water of egotistical calculation. "All that is solid melts into air." Read asking whether this description of modernity feels more like a critique or an accurate diagnosis, and whether Marx thought it could be reversed.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Manifesto through the lens of the cash nexus argument — the claim that bourgeois society dissolves all traditional bonds into market relations — and ask whether this is a sociological observation, a moral critique, or both, and what follows from it.

cast.name: The Bourgeoisie
cast.description: The class that owns the means of production — factories, capital, the world market. Marx credits the bourgeoisie with more revolutionary energy than any class in history: it destroyed feudalism, created the global economy, and pulled every nation into modernity. That same energy, he argues, has produced the conditions for its own overthrow.

cast.name: The Proletariat
cast.description: The class that sells its labour for wages — the industrial working class produced by the same machinery that made the bourgeoisie powerful. The Manifesto's central claim: the proletariat is the first class in history whose liberation requires the abolition of all classes, including itself. It is the bourgeoisie's gravedigger.

cast.name: Class Struggle
cast.description: The first sentence of Part I is the thesis: the history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles. Freeman and slave, patrician and plebeian, lord and serf — every era is defined by the antagonism between those who own the conditions of production and those who must work within them.

cast.name: The Cash Nexus
cast.description: Marx's term for the transformation wrought by the bourgeoisie: every human relationship — religious devotion, family loyalty, professional honour — has been drowned in the icy water of egotistical calculation. "All that is solid melts into air." The cash nexus is not a side effect of capitalism; it is its defining social logic.

cast.name: The Communist
cast.description: Not a separate party with separate interests, but the most advanced section of the working class — those who understand the historical direction of the movement and can articulate its long-term aims. The Communists do not form a sect; they push forward what the conditions of history have already made inevitable.

cast.name: Revolution
cast.description: Not a choice but a historical necessity — the point at which the contradictions of capitalist society become irresolvable by reform. The bourgeoisie cannot stop producing the proletariat, and the proletariat cannot be free within the existing order. The Manifesto ends with a call: workers of all countries, unite.

whyItMatters.title: History as Class Struggle
whyItMatters.body: The Manifesto argues that history is the story of class conflict — between masters and slaves, lords and serfs, factory owners and workers. The framework has shaped historical thinking far beyond communism. Even readers who reject Marx's conclusions have found his question — who profits from this arrangement? — productive.

whyItMatters.title: Capitalism's Own Logic
whyItMatters.body: Marx and Engels were among the first to see capitalism not as a fixed system but as a dynamic process — concentrating capital, dissolving traditional structures, creating global markets, reshaping every relationship into a transaction. Much of their description of capitalism still reads accurately.

whyItMatters.title: A Document That Changed History
whyItMatters.body: The Manifesto did not remain theory. Revolutions in Russia, China, Cuba, and elsewhere were made in its name. The 20th century cannot be understood without it. Reading it is reading the source of an immense amount of what happened next, both terrible and aspiring.
